title: Israel tightens election safeguards as public distrust surges: What to know
gist: Ahead of Israel's Oct. 27, 2026 election -- the first since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack, and a razor-thin race between Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party -- public distrust in election integrity has jumped from 25% to 70% in under four years, driving new AI-content labeling rules, a ban on app-based voter tracking, and a 100,000-volunteer civil-society monitoring effort.

insights.claim: A Kan public broadcaster poll found Prime Minister Netanyahu's Likud and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's new Yashar party each projected to win 23 Knesset seats in Israel's October 27, 2026 election, making it an effective dead heat for the largest-party title.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A near-tied race raises the stakes of any electoral irregularity or misinformation event; expect elevated political-risk pricing on Israeli assets into and immediately after October 27.
insights.quote: the ruling Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party would each win 23 Knesset seats

insights.claim: In such a close race, even small-scale manipulation of results could be decisive, according to Israel Democracy Institute researcher Tamar Hermann.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: Frames electoral-integrity risk as a market-relevant tail risk given how tight the Likud-Yashar race is, not just an abstract democratic-norms concern.
insights.quote: The battle over who becomes Israel's largest party could be determined by a handful of votes. This means that even a rather small-scale manipulation of the results could be decisive
insights.locator: quote from Hermann on the Kan poll

insights.claim: Public trust in Israel's election integrity has collapsed: an Israel Democracy Institute study published August 5, 2026 found 70% of respondents believe there is a threat to election integrity, up from only 25% in a comparable poll before the November 2022 election.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A near-tripling of distrust in under four years is itself a political-stability indicator; sustained delegitimization risk regardless of the actual vote outcome, which can prolong post-election uncertainty and government-formation friction.
insights.quote: 70% of respondents believed there was a threat to the integrity of Israel's elections

insights.claim: Central Elections Committee Chairman Judge Noam Solberg published new instructions on August 4, 2026 banning political party representatives at polling stations from using apps to report the identities of specific voters, ruling the practice violates voters' privacy rights.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: Shows regulators are actively closing known intimidation/surveillance vectors ahead of the vote, a positive signal for process integrity that partially offsets the trust-collapse narrative.

insights.claim: Israel has enacted a legal requirement mandating that campaign content created or substantially altered using artificial intelligence be labeled, specifically to address AI-driven election manipulation.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: An early real-world case study of AI-content labeling law applied to a national election -- relevant precedent for regulatory approaches likely to spread to other democracies facing generative-AI election risk.

insights.claim: Tamar Hermann identifies two distinct AI-driven election threats: manipulated content and bots spreading fake news during the campaign, and AI-generated content designed to create panic specifically on election day itself.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A useful two-bucket framework (pre-vote narrative manipulation vs. election-day panic content) for assessing AI election risk in any democracy, not just Israel.
insights.quote: manipulated content and bots spreading fake news during the election campaign, and AI-generated content potentially creating panic on election day
insights.locator: quote from Hermann on AI threats

insights.claim: Fear of AI manipulation and cyberattacks is a specific reason Israel has chosen to retain paper ballots instead of adopting a computerized voting system.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A concrete case of AI-risk concerns actively reversing a country's push toward electronic voting -- a signal that could inform similar policy debates elsewhere.
insights.quote: The risks posed by AI manipulation and cyberattacks are among the reasons why Israel opted to maintain paper ballots instead of using a computerized voting system
insights.locator: quote from Hermann on paper ballots

insights.claim: According to a June 2025 Times of Israel report, since Itamar Ben-Gvir was appointed national security minister in December 2022, police have taken a tougher stance toward protesters generally except right-wing activists, many of whom were filmed committing severe political violence but not investigated, while anti-government and Arab protesters were violently arrested, in some cases for trivial offenses or without justification.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: An asymmetric policing pattern feeding directly into the 70% distrust figure; if this asymmetry persists into the election period it raises real risk of contested legitimacy for the winning outcome, especially if Likud (Ben-Gvir's coalition partner) wins narrowly.
insights.locator: paragraph citing June 2025 Times of Israel report

insights.claim: Mordechai David, a right-wing activist known for confronting and heckling leftist figures, journalists, politicians and judicial officials, has been questioned by police multiple times but released without charge each time, cited by civil-society organizers as evidence police tolerate anti-democratic intimidation.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A concrete named case study organizers use to argue enforcement is selectively lenient toward pro-government-aligned actors -- a specific fact pattern worth tracking if it recurs closer to the election.

insights.claim: Election Command Center co-founder Michal Beinisch warned that police tolerance of intimidation incidents combined with legislation eroding judicial powers signals the election campaign and election day itself could come under attack from anti-democratic forces, compounded by radicalized social-media and parliamentary discourse.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A civil-society leader explicitly links judicial-power erosion legislation to election-day risk -- worth watching as a leading indicator for post-election contestation or unrest.
insights.quote: Police tolerance toward such incidents and legislation eroding the powers of the judicial system are all indications that the election campaign and election day could be under attack by anti-democratic forces

insights.claim: The Election Command Center, founded roughly nine months before the article (around late 2025) by Michal Beinisch and Eyal Naveh and headquartered in Herzliya, runs 300 volunteers monitoring defamatory content and a separate 150-volunteer digital department searching for false or inciting narratives online.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: A 450-person volunteer content-monitoring operation is a meaningful, scaled civil-society check on disinformation ahead of the vote -- a mitigant to weigh against the distrust and AI-risk narrative.
insights.locator: paragraph on Herzliya headquarters and volunteer counts

insights.claim: The Election Command Center's polling-station monitoring app, launched about a week before the article, had already been downloaded more than 30,000 times, with the group targeting 100,000 volunteers nationwide by election day (October 27).
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: Rapid uptake (30,000 downloads in about a week) signals significant public appetite for grassroots election monitoring, itself a proxy indicator of how seriously Israelis are treating integrity risk this cycle.
insights.quote: More than 30,000 people have already downloaded the app
insights.locator: paragraph on app launch and downloads

insights.claim: Election Command Center co-founder Eyal Naveh said the group's monitoring efforts are already producing a measurable decrease in defamation, fake news and hateful speech online, tracked via frequency of hateful keywords and attacks on targeted public figures' profiles.
insights.speaker: Rina Bassist
insights.so_what: If the group's self-reported metrics hold up, it suggests organized civil monitoring can measurably dampen disinformation volume ahead of a contested vote -- a template potentially exportable to other election-integrity efforts.
insights.quote: We are already seeing results, with a clear decrease in defamation, fake news and hateful speech on the web
insights.locator: quote from Naveh near end of article
